title: Blessing others
hookLine: the Guru asks for the dust of the feet of the Sikh who remembers and helps others remember (Gauri Var M4, ang 306)

cards: Shoes come off at the door of a gurdwara. In some gurdwaras, volunteers take them, line them up, even wipe the dust off, and the person doing it might be a shopkeeper, a student, or someone with a great deal of money.
Dust from other people's feet, handled as an honor. Hold that picture, because Guru Ram Das ends his salok about the Gursikh's day with dust. And the surprise is who's asking for it.

teach.h: SERVANT NANAK ASKS FOR THE DUST.
THE GURU BOWS TO THE DISCIPLE.
teach.b: The one on whom my Lord is kind, to that Gursikh the Guru gives the teaching. Servant Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of that Gursikh who repeats the Name himself, and leads others to repeat it.
Read it slowly; it turns things upside down. The voice is the Guru's, signing with the name Nanak, as the Gurus do in the Granth, and calling himself servant.
And the Guru is the one asking, for the dust of a disciple's feet. Touching someone's feet is a gesture of deep respect in Punjab. Asking for the dust from them goes lower still.
Next, notice which Sikh he honors this way. The earlier lines already called the Sikh who rises early and remembers through the working day pleasing to the Guru's mind.
But the one whose dust the Guru asks for remembers and then helps someone else remember. The salok has been walking outward all along: one person waking, a day of work, other people.
And the first line says the teaching comes as kindness. The Gursikh doesn't earn it like a wage.
The Lord is kind, and the Guru shares the teaching. So helping someone remember isn't a lecture or a recruiting drive.
It's passing on a kindness you were given: a reminder on a hard day, a line of a hymn sent to a friend, an invitation to sit together.

how: Sikhs meet this salok when Gauri ki Var is sung or read, and it is quoted when Sikhs speak of the Gursikh's day; looking after shoes at the gurdwara door is one of the forms of seva Sikhs volunteer for.

o: helping someone else remember the Name, as a kindness
a priest's blessing given at the end of prayers
sprinkling holy water on guests at the door

games.q: the salok's last lines: tap the pairs.

s: in the salok, the Sikh asks the Guru for the dust of his feet
it's the other way around: servant Nanak asks for the dust of the Gursikh's feet.
the Gursikh honored at the end is the one who also helps others remember
the one who repeats the Name himself and leads others to repeat it.
the salok says the teaching is a wage for rising early
it comes to the one on whom the Lord is kind.

games.q: a Sikh rises early, remembers through the workday, and then helps a friend remember too. what does the salok's last line do?
o: tells the Sikh to bow lower.
has the Guru ask for that Sikh's dust.
games.why: servant Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of that Gursikh: the blessing runs from the Guru to the disciple.

practice: Let one person come to mind who could use a reminder today, of something good, of someone who loves them, of a line that once steadied you.
Without planning a speech, find one small, kind way to pass it on, a message, a call, a line of Gurbani if they'd welcome it, and if you pray, hold them in Waheguru for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Blessing others. The salok's last line: servant Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of the Sikh who remembers the Name and helps others remember it. Today's word.

orig.note: dust: in the salok, the dust of a Gursikh's feet, asked for by the Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: help others remember. A kindness you were given is meant to travel. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Gauri ki Var, salok Mahala 4, Ang 306 (the Guru gives the teaching to the one on whom the Lord is kind; servant Nanak asks for the dust of the Gursikh who repeats the Name and leads others to repeat it)
